query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Short-range chemical ordering at or near grain boundaries in a single-phase, compositionally complex alloy can locally reduce boundary cohesion under certain stress and temperature conditions, leading to brittle behavior even in the absence of large-scale second-phase precipitation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, nominally single-phase high-entropy (compositionally complex) alloy with an FCC matrix and minimal precipitates or segregation, suitable for demanding engineering service.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to integrated in-situ mechanical testing and advanced diffraction/imaging, combined with atomistic simulations, to detect and track local short-range order formation under varied stress states and temperatures.
generation.conditions: Test across a range of service-relevant temperatures (from cryogenic to elevated) and strain rates; employ inert/environmentally controlled setups to avoid confounding effects from oxidation or hydrogen embrittlement.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized short-range chemical order clusters forming at or near grain boundaries that lower effective cohesive strength.
generation.mechanism: During deformation at lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates, dynamic formation of short-range order near grain boundaries raises localized stress concentrations and weakens these interfaces, triggering intergranular or cleavage-like fracture. Conventional single-phase alloys with simpler compositions do not typically form such extensive ordering that promotes brittle boundary failure under comparable conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-homogenized baseline with high ductility and toughness, the onset of short-range ordering near grain boundaries is expected to correlate with a drop in fracture toughness and an increased propensity for boundary cracks. Conventional alloys of similar grain size and no strong short-range order should show milder toughness degradation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: In conventional alloys, grain-boundary precipitation and coarse particle formation are the known primary routes to toughness loss, whereas in compositionally complex single-phase alloys the local short-range order can drive embrittlement even in the absence of coarse precipitates.
generation.boundary: Above a critical temperature, short-range order effects are substantially mitigated by diffusion, restoring higher ductility; at very low strain rates or significantly higher temperatures, boundary brittleness from SRO is diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The extent and kinetics of short-range order formation, as well as possible synergy with minor impurity segregation, remain insufficiently constrained and require further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple batches of the same compositionally complex alloy in a single-phase, homogenized condition. Subject them to in-situ tensile or fracture toughness measurements at successively lower temperatures and higher strain rates while performing high-resolution diffraction and microscopy to detect short-range order near grain boundaries. Compare to a control set of conventional single-phase alloys under the same conditions.
measurements: Synchrotron or neutron diffraction signals to identify short-range order evolution in real time
Atom probe tomography or high-resolution electron microscopy to pinpoint local boundary composition changes
Fractography to assess intergranular vs. transgranular fracture modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under conditions where brittle behavior is observed, there is no detectable short-range order near grain boundaries, or if measured toughness and fracture modes do not differ between the compositionally complex alloy and conventional single-phase systems, the hypothesis is invalidated.

In contrast to carbides and nitrides, intermetallic compound–induced embrittlement at room temperature can be relieved at high temperatures because plastic codeformation between these compounds and the matrix can reduce stress concentration and, thus, delay crack initiation (). Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
